title: PPLE Skills and Research Methods for Psychology: tutorial manual
text:
Preface
Welcome! In these pages you will find tutorial materials for the PPLE Skills and Research Methods for Psychology tutorials. In session 2025/26, we will be working with JASP (JASP Team, 2025) which can be downloaded here.
Every tutorial page features video demonstrations which are often based on examples presented in the course textbook, Discovering Statistics using JASP (Field et al., 2025), and the accompanying datasets prepared by Andy Field. All of these datasets can be downloaded directly from the textbook’s companion website.
Although not part of the course this year, code to run the featured analyses in the R programming language (R Core Team, 2025) will also be included, for the curious.
For questions, please get in touch!

title: 2  Bias and checking assumptions
text:
2.4 Guide to diagnostic plots

2.4.1 Boxplot







Note 2.1: How to interpret a boxplot




Blue box spans the middle 50% of the data
Q1 (25th percentile) distinguishes lower 25% of the sorted values
Median (Q2/50th percentile) splits the sorted dataset in half
Q3 (75th percentile) distinguishes the upper 25% of the sorted values
Potential outliers are identified by the ‘boxplot rule’ whereby a value is flagged if it is smaller/larger than the value of Q1/Q3 minus/plus 1.5 times the interquartile range
The vertical lines at the end of the whiskers show the minimum and maximum values in the absence of outliers

If there are no visible whiskers and no outliers, then the minimum and maximum are respectively equal to Q1 and Q3






2.4.2 QQ and density/distribution plots
In the figure below you can see the impact of different types of deviation from normality on how data appear in QQ and density plots. Note the correspondence between the sample quantiles and the theoretical quantiles in the case of the (near) normal distribution, and how this correspondence varies in the skewed or non-mesokurtic distributions underneath.

title: Appendix B — The impact of assumption violations on test results
text:
B.1 Normality
Although we have discussed checking for bias in the model, you will likely have noticed that assumption tests are very rarely reported in the psychological literature, which could lead you to question the influence that assumption violations have on inference.
Normally, we do not know whether \(H_0\) or \(H_1\) is true, but simulations allow us to fix “population” parameters and then draw samples to investigate how robust our hypothesis tests are against assumption violations. For example, we can look at whether independent-samples t-tests produce results in line with our given \(\alpha\) level by repeatedly drawing groups from a simulated population where \(\mu\) = 0 (i.e., where both groups come from the same null population where there is no treatment effect) and calculating the proportion of significant test results. On the other hand, we can determine whether the power of a test is in line with expectations by drawing groups from populations with different values of \(\mu\), and counting the instances where the test detected the “true” effect.

title: 4  ANCOVA and (between-subjects) factorial ANOVA
text:
4.2 Datasets
This demonstration uses the datasets goggles and puppy_love which were prepared by Andy Field and included in Field, van Doorn and Wagenmakers (2025).
goggles contains (fictional) data from a 2 x 3 factorial design with 2 between-subjects IVs. IV1 is attractiveness of face stimulus (Attractive or Unattractive) and IV2 is dosage of alcohol (Placebo, Low, or High). Participants were assigned to either the placebo, low dose, or high does group and gave attractiveness ratings (DV) to either attractive or unattractive faces.
puppy_love contains (fictional) data from a design with one, 3-level, between-subjects IV (dose of puppies: Control, 15 minutes, and 30 minutes of puppy therapy) and one DV (Happiness after therapy, 0-10). The dataset also includes the covariate Love of puppies measured on a scale of 0-7.

title: 5  ANOVAs for repeated measures and mixed designs
text:
5.2 Datasets
This demonstration uses the dataset PastryBirdsMixed which you can download here. The file contains (fictional) data which look at sausage roll (saucijzenbroodje) preference in birds from the Corvid family. This is a 3 x 2 x 2 mixed design: IV1 (between-subjects) is Bird (Crow, Jackdaw, or Magpie); IV2 (within-subjects) is Baker (Albert Heijn/AH or Kiosk); IV3 (within-subjects) is Filling (Meat or Vegatarian). The DV is the number of times the bird pecked at the sausage roll upon presentation.

title: 8  Moderation and Mediation

8.2 Datasets
The moderation demonstration uses the dataset video_games which was prepared by Andy Field and included in Field, van Doorn and Wagenmakers (2025). The dataset includes the variables Aggression (DV), Video games (hours per week) (IV1), and Callous Unemotional Traits (IV2/Moderator).
The mediation demonstration uses the dataset lambert_2012 which is based on data from the study of Lambert et al. (2012) on pornography use and infidelity, and is included in Field, van Doorn and Wagenmakers (2025). IV1 is Porn consumption (log-transformed), IV2 (the mediator) is Relationship commitment, and the DV is Physical infidelity.
